summary: Grid optimisation, exploration, and the datacenter power crunch make energy both an AI user and AI's binding constraint. Who tracks it: the utility research bodies and DOE are the primary record, with the grid and oilfield incumbents' own technology programs layered on top.

analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey recorded 12.6% of utilities firms actively using AI in its latest reading, down from 17.1% in the prior period, though the Census note covers utilities under NAICS 22 while oil and gas extraction reports separately under mining, so the headline figure understates the broader energy sector's activity. Across both grid-side and upstream operations, AI deployment is well established rather than experimental, with major operators, equipment vendors, and specialist software companies each playing a distinct role in a layered market.

On the grid side, the Department of Energy's AI office frames the technology as central to grid security, scientific discovery, and energy independence, and its Grid Modernization Initiative coordinates federal and national laboratory work on real-time grid balancing, reactor optimization, and carbon capture across US utilities. The Electric Power Research Institute runs the sector's shared research layer, with working groups specifically focused on AI grid resilience, wildfire-risk prediction, and asset-health monitoring. IEEE PES, which produces nearly half of all IEEE standards annually, sets the technical and interoperability standards for machine learning in power systems, grid cyber-defense, and distributed energy resource management, giving operators a standards framework that industrial AI in many other sectors still lacks.

Forecasting is one of the clearest places where AI delivers a measurable operational edge. Amperon, founded in 2018 and built around a former energy trader and data engineer, uses machine learning across 40,000 weather points from four vendors, analyzing roughly 25 weather variables every hour with an ensemble model drawing from three weather vendors, and claims its models produce load, price, and renewable forecasts up to 3x more accurate than conventional approaches and regularly beat ISO forecasts. NextEra Energy, described as America's largest electric utility and one of the nation's top wholesale generators, applies AI to wind and solar yield forecasting, battery dispatch optimization, and automated plant maintenance across its renewable fleet. Siemens Energy ships AI controllers and digital-twin software for gas, wind, and grid assets, positioning AI as something that arrives embedded in equipment rather than as a separate software purchase.

In upstream oil and gas, Baker Hughes describes its portfolio as enriched by digitalization, artificial intelligence, and automation capabilities that enable remote operations, reduce risk, and drive decarbonization, with industrial solutions that surface critical insights across asset, process, and sustainability performance. Geoteric applies deep learning directly to 3D seismic data, offering automated subsurface fault mapping for exploration and production workflows through its AI Hub platform, with one operator stating the technology is revolutionizing upstream exploration efforts and will help digitize and decarbonize operations globally.

Energy is unusual among AI-adopting sectors because it is simultaneously a heavy user of AI and the binding physical constraint on AI's expansion everywhere else. Per DOE, data centers consumed about 4.4% of US electricity in 2023, projected to reach 6.7 to 12% by 2028, with AI identified as the primary driver, and DOE has separately stated that data centers are projected to consume up to 9% of total US electricity demand by 2030. DOE has responded with a Speed to Power Initiative to accelerate large-scale grid infrastructure development and announced plans to partner with private-sector developers to build AI data centers and energy-generation projects on DOE lands. DOE also acknowledges the risk side plainly, noting that AI systems may generate incorrect, unverifiable, and potentially harmful outputs and that any use must properly understand and mitigate those risks, a posture that reflects the sector's sensitivity to grid reliability and safety.

For an operator or investor evaluating deployment, the evidence in these sources suggests that forecasting accuracy, predictive maintenance, and seismic interpretation are the applications with the clearest demonstrated value and the most mature vendor ecosystems. Federal programs through DOE and the Grid Modernization Initiative provide both co-investment opportunities and a policy environment actively pushing adoption for grid resilience and decarbonization. The drop in the Census adoption rate between periods is a caution worth noting, though whether it reflects genuine pullback, survey timing, or the sector's uneven coverage across NAICS codes is not resolved by the available data.
